sections.text: To plan a SIP for a child's education, size it from the future cost, not today's. A degree that costs Rs. 20 lakh today costs about Rs. 94.3 lakh in 18 years if education costs rise 9% a year (20 lakh times 1.09 to the power 18), and saving that amount takes roughly Rs. 12,325 a month from the child's birth at an assumed 12% return. Both the 9% and the 12% are assumptions you should vary, because the answer is very sensitive to each of them.
Step 1: Pick an inflation assumption and test it

There is no single correct education inflation rate, and it differs by course and institution, so this post treats it as an input rather than a fact. The table works out the target in 18 years for a Rs. 20 lakh course today, and the monthly SIP needed at two return assumptions, using the SIP calculator's method (monthly rate = annual rate divided by 12, instalments at the start of each month, instalment = target divided by the future value of Rs. 1 a month).

Check on the 9% and 12% case: Rs. 12,325 a month for 216 months grows to Rs. 94.3 lakh in the calculator, with Rs. 26.6 lakh paid in. The gap between the best and worst corner of the table is almost 2.5 times in SIP size, so plan with the cautious corner and revisit every year.
Step 2: Know what starting late costs
The target date does not move, so a late start squeezes the same goal into fewer months. Three years of delay raises the instalment by about half. It takes a five-year delay to double it.
Step 3: Remember the bills arrive over several years

Most courses charge fees each year, not in one payment at 18. Suppose the Rs. 20 lakh is Rs. 5 lakh a year in today's money over four years. At 9% inflation the four payments, made at ages 18 to 21, are Rs. 23,58,560, Rs. 25,70,831, Rs. 28,02,205 and Rs. 30,54,404, totalling Rs. 1.08 crore. If the unspent balance earns 7% after the child turns 18, you need about Rs. 97.0 lakh on the 18th birthday to meet all four, which takes around Rs. 12,675 a month at 12%. The total is higher than the single-payment target because later payments are inflated for longer.
Step 4: Protect the last few years

A goal with a fixed date cannot wait for a market to recover. Using the Rs. 12,325 plan, the balance at the end of year 17 is Rs. 82.3 lakh. If an equity-heavy holding then fell 30% (a hypothetical shock, not a forecast) and the year-18 instalments continued, the corpus would reach only about Rs. 66.5 lakh, around 71% of the Rs. 94.3 lakh needed. Moving to lower-risk holdings earlier reduces this risk but also lowers growth: if the plan earns 12% for 15 years and 6% for the last 3, the instalment must rise to about Rs. 14,664 a month, roughly 19% more, to reach the same target.

On the Rs. 12,325 plan at a steady 12%, the balance should read about Rs. 5.36 lakh after 3 years, Rs. 13.03 lakh after 6, Rs. 24.01 lakh after 9, Rs. 39.72 lakh after 12 and Rs. 62.19 lakh after 15, against Rs. 4.44 lakh, Rs. 8.87 lakh, Rs. 13.31 lakh, Rs. 17.75 lakh and Rs. 22.19 lakh paid in. Real balances will wander around these figures. If you fall well behind at the halfway mark, raise the instalment then, because the cost of catching up grows every year you wait.

items: Using today's course fee as the target. At 9% a year, prices multiply by 4.7 in 18 years.
Mixing goals. Put education in its own SIP so that a withdrawal for another purpose does not leave a gap in a fixed-date goal.
Assuming a straight-line 12%. Equity-oriented funds can fall sharply, and returns are not guaranteed. Run the plan at 8% and 10% as well.

Not stepping up. If the first instalment is a stretch, a yearly increase can start the plan lower. A 10% yearly step-up needs about Rs. 6,545 to start in the 9% inflation, 12% return case, with Rs. 35.8 lakh paid in over 18 years.

Ignoring the course type. Fees for studying abroad, professional programmes and local degrees can differ widely, and currency moves add risk when the course is abroad. Use a cost quote for the course you actually have in mind.
